vignette:
She is 44, a Latin American woman who has spent most of her adult life inside the routines of religious life. As a nun, she is used to structure: morning prayer before dawn, shared meals eaten quietly, catechism classes with children from the neighborhood, visits to older parishioners, evenings folded back into silence. Before the attack, she experiences her vocation as steadying. She likes the predictability of convent life and the sense that even suffering can be met with purpose. She is divorced, a part of her history she rarely speaks about directly, but she once tells it as evidence that she has already survived one life falling apart and built another from faith.

The traumatic event happens three years ago, on an ordinary weekday afternoon. She is at a parish outreach center run by her order, helping prepare food bags and organizing donated school supplies. Children are moving in and out of the courtyard, and two other sisters are nearby. She remembers hearing what she first takes for construction noise from the street, then shouting, then the concussive force of an explosion that seems to rip the air open. Windows burst inward. Dust and glass fill the room. A second blast follows close enough that she cannot tell where her body ends and the sound begins. She falls to the floor and tastes blood, though later she realizes it comes from a cut inside her mouth. Someone is screaming prayers in Spanish. A child is crying for his mother. When she tries to stand, her legs shake so hard that she crawls instead.

The attack is later described on the news as an act of terrorism targeting a government building nearby, but at the time she knows only chaos. In fragments, she remembers seeing one of the sisters with blood on her veil, a sandal lying by itself near the doorway, smoke swallowing the courtyard where children had been running only minutes before. She spends hours afterward moving between stunned action and disbelief, helping where she can, calling names, pressing cloth against wounds with trembling hands. That night, in a hospital corridor, she cannot stop watching the entrance, convinced another blast is coming.

In the weeks after, everyone around her speaks of gratitude that she survived. She says the right things. God protected us. We must remain strong for the community. But sleep changes almost immediately. When she closes her eyes, she is back under the force of the blast, hearing the crack of glass and the high-pitched ringing that came after. Sometimes the dreams are exact; sometimes they shift, and in them she cannot find the children. She starts waking before dawn gasping, one hand clutched to her chest. At morning prayer she loses her place in familiar passages. A slammed door or a motorcycle backfiring on the street makes her duck and cover her head before she can think.

She returns to her duties because that is what she knows to do, but her world becomes organized around avoiding reminders. She no longer wants to work in the outreach center courtyard. If a crowd gathers outside the church, she finds reasons to stay in the office. Public events, processions, holiday masses-once central to her work-now fill her with dread. She scans every entrance, every unattended bag, every stranger who lingers too long. During confession hours she catches herself studying people's hands and jackets instead of hearing their words. She is ashamed of this. She tells herself that a woman of faith should trust more and fear less, but the fear arrives faster than belief.

The hardest part for her is what the trauma does to her sense of calling. She says she used to feel close to people's pain; now she feels herself pulling away from it. When children run noisily through the parish hall, she stiffens instead of smiling. When mothers ask for help, she sometimes feels irritated by their urgency and then hates herself for it. She avoids the sister who was injured in the attack because being near her brings back the smell of dust and blood. On anniversaries or after news of bombings elsewhere, she becomes withdrawn and silent, eating little, speaking only when necessary. The other sisters notice she spends more time alone in the chapel, though even there she does not feel peaceful. She sits rigid in the pew, listening for danger.

She also carries a private burden of guilt. She thinks of the children who were there that day and replays small decisions-why she went to the supply room, why she did not move faster, whether she should have done more for the wounded. Intellectually she knows she could not have stopped the attack, but her mind keeps returning to the same impossible bargains. She says that before, prayer felt like conversation; now it often feels like argument. She asks God why some lived and others did not. She asks why she is still frightened in places that are supposed to be sacred.

Now, three years later, her life appears orderly from the outside. She keeps her schedule, teaches classes, attends services, answers warmly when spoken to. But she lives with constant tension under the surface. She sleeps lightly and wakes at small sounds. She avoids news footage of explosions yet cannot stop imagining them. In crowded spaces she positions herself near exits. She has become, in her words, "a person always bracing." What troubles her most is that the attack is not past in the way other memories are past. It remains immediate, waiting inside noise, dust, crowds, and silence, ready to take hold of her body before her mind can catch up.
